doc.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
title: Meeting touring stars at neighbors' parties; the autograph book
summary: A neighborhood promoter and the Hills hosted visiting artists like Lena Horne, Billy Eckstine and Marian Anderson, and young Walton collected autographs, living by segregation's two-way rules.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: There was a gentleman around the corner named uh, last name was Lewis who brought in uh, uh, the artists, you know. I mean, he was a promoter. So there was inevitably a party in his yard for these people who came to Dallas to perform, and I would, uh, you know, go next door and see who it was, you know, any person of interest. A lot of times uh, Rhythm & Blues artists and my interest was minimal.

But uh, people like Lena Horne or Billy Eckstine, Marian Anderson, were hosted to a, shall we say, a, a reception at the uh, the Hill's residence which was two doors down, a little nearer to me than this person I was telling you about that did booking. And at a given moment, they would, they would call me and say, "Okay Billy, you can come now," and I'd go with my autograph book. And they'd say, …

…"Ah, isn't he cute," you know. "Ah, he's such a doll." Oh man, I went crazy. I had a great autograph book. I can't find it now though. Makes me want to cry, you know. But not on camera, on camera … I won't do that. But uh, yeah, that was, so that would give you an idea of how we uh, existed in the two-way rules of segregation.
